entities.name: Aspar
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aspar (c. 400–471 CE) was an Alanic-Gothic general (magister militum) and patrician who wielded immense political and military power in the Eastern Roman Empire during the mid-5th century. Operating from Constantinople, he was a kingmaker, instrumental in the ascension of emperors Marcian and Leo I, demonstrating the profound influence foreign-born military commanders could exert over the imperial court in an era increasingly dependent on Germanic auxiliaries. His career reflects the complex ethnic and religious dynamics within the late Roman state, as an Arian Christian commanding a predominantly Orthodox empire.

Aspar's military career saw him serve under Theodosius II, participating in campaigns against the Huns and the Sasanian Empire. His political zenith arrived in 457 CE when, despite his Arian faith preventing him from taking the purple himself, he orchestrated the elevation of Marcian, followed by Leo I. Aspar's sons, Ardabur and Patricius, also held significant military commands, solidifying the family's grip on power. Notably, he led a disastrous naval expedition against the Vandal Kingdom in Africa in 468 CE, a catastrophic failure that severely weakened the Eastern Empire's resources and prestige, though his exact culpability remains debated among historians.

His ultimate downfall came in 471 CE, when Emperor Leo I, weary of Aspar's overarching influence and his Arian beliefs, orchestrated his assassination along with his son Ardabur. This dramatic purge marked a pivotal moment in Eastern Roman history, signifying a conscious effort by the imperial authority to diminish Germanic influence within the military and court, paving the way for the rise of Isaurian generals like Zeno. Aspar's demise underscored the precarious balance between imperial sovereignty and the power of ambitious military leaders, contributing to the distinct trajectory of the Eastern Empire compared to its Western counterpart.
